doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 17, 2022 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Joining Sun Ra's band in New York via the euphonium player
summary: Harrison, about 20-21 and newly arrived from Detroit, explains he was introduced to Sun Ra by a euphonium and trombone player, rehearsed at Sun Ra's house and was told to forget changes.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: I’m fascinated and curious about Sun Ra and I wanted to ask you, you entered that band for however many gigs you did as obviously one of the newcomers and you were sitting next to people like Marshall Allen, who had been there since the get-go. Did you get advice from the band members as well as Sun Ra about how to fit into whatever it is they were doing?

Yes. Yes. I was a young guy at that time. I think I was about 20, 21 years old, and I had just gotten, I had just arrived from Detroit. My first engagement was with Grant Green and I was working around, and we would tour, but on the off weeks I would play with Sun Ra. I was introduced to Sun Ra by a euphonium and trombone player, Kiwami Ziti

Kiwami. K-I-N-I-B-I [misspelled] Ziwati. And we were staying together in the loft on Broadway, 89 E Broadway Street. And all kinds of people would come by and sessions, and we studied, actually we were vegetarians at the time. And so he called Kiwami to come in and play for a few gigs and whatnot, and Sun Ra asked Kiwami did he know of a saxophone player. So Kiwami recommended me, because Pharoah had went with — Pharoah was doing presentations and performances with Sun Ra as well, but he had worked with Trane. John Gilmore had went with Art Blakey at the time. So there was a vacancy. So I made a rehearsal. Sun Ra stayed on Third Street, not too far from Avenue A. And I went over to Sun Ra’s house and he was cooking for the band. He was like of like an old grandmother you know, he was cooking for the band and it was like collard greens and black eyed peas and whatnot, real southern cuisine, because you know he’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

from Alabama basically, by way of Chicago. So I didn’t really eat that much because I was so excited about playing with the group that I’d never played that way before. I’d never played that free style before you know. So when I started playing he told me to forget about changes, just think about the sound and imagery you know. Let your imagination take control.
